interest: Salvadoran rumors of Japanese bases and bribery in the mid-1930s.
overview: This State Department file (decimal file 894.20216) documents U.S. diplomatic and military intelligence monitoring of Japanese activities in El Salvador between 1935 and 1940. Key subjects include allegations that President Maximiliano Hernández Martínez's regime sought to purchase Japanese armaments and negotiate naval and provisioning base rights for Japan in the Gulf of Fonseca near the Panama Canal, as well as rumors that high Salvadoran officials were being suborned by Japanese funds. The documents trace the establishment of Japan's first diplomatic legation in San Salvador under Chargé d'Affaires Yashichi Otani, public and media agitation surrounding visiting Japanese trade diplomats investigating Central American customs tariffs, the circulation of Japanese propaganda regarding the Sino-Japanese conflict, and surveillance indicating minimal Japanese resident presence in the country by late 1940.

subfiles.about: Internal State Department memorandum summarizing a report that Salvadoran officials were being suborned by Japanese money.

subfiles.about: Confidential despatch reporting allegations of Salvadoran officials receiving Japanese bribes and the opening of the Japanese Legation in San Salvador.
subfiles.summary: Corrigan reports claims that Japanese money was bribing Salvadoran officials and that El Salvador was becoming a center of Japanese activity.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 568 on Japanese Activities and the Japanese Legation in San Salvador

subfiles.about: Newspaper article reporting an unsuccessful attempt by a reporter to interview two secretive Japanese visitors at the Hotel Nuevo Mundo.
